narratives.narrative: The psalter's opening word weighs a whole human life and pronounces it happy (101 'blessed is the man'; 102 affect): beatitude is not a feeling that flares but the settled well-being (106) carried by the blessed man himself (105) — the bearer who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, delights in the law, and prospers like a watered tree. The movement is inward and terminal: its locus is an interior state (116 internal:ib-state), its target simply the beatitude it names (107), and its coupling is blessedness as such (112). The silences are eloquent — no source is recorded (103 absent), no seat (104 none), no manner, no intensity, no effect, no prohibition: this happiness is not lodged in a bodily organ, is not graded up or down, produces no further downstream act, and is forbidden to no one. It is read as a role-bearing characteristic (115), a state the whole shaped life simply is rather than does.
narratives.variation_note: The Psalter's opening esher-beatitude and the archetype of the whole item: among the H0835 readings this one grounds happiness in a whole way of life (avoidance of the wicked's counsel joined to delight in the law), not in a single footing like forgiveness (32:1), trust (40:4), the fear of God (112:1), discipline (94:12), or prosperity (144:15) — the foundational, comprehensive beatitude the later readings each narrow.

narratives.narrative: Against the taunt hurled at the psalmist's very soul in v2 ('there is no salvation for him in God'), the interior lands, at the close, on the opposite settled conviction: salvation belongs to the LORD (101; 102 cognition). This is a movement of the mind — the self (105) settling its own theology of rescue (106), confessing (107) what it now holds as certain, the confession coupled to the conviction that salvation is God's alone (112). The absences frame it: no source is named (103), no seat (104 none) — the conviction is not organ-lodged; no manner, intensity, effect or prohibition. That effect-silence matters — the confession is offered as an end in itself, the interior at rest in what it knows, not as a lever to a further outcome. Locus is internal (116): the drama is entirely a change of mind inside the man, God the arena it now trusts.

Here blessing runs outward from the human interior toward God: 'I bless the LORD who gives me counsel' (101; 102 affect). The self (105) performs the operation of blessing the God who guides it (106), the act a grateful-blessing (107) specifically coupled to the counsel received (112 bless-for-counsel) — gratitude aimed not at rescue but at being advised, with the night-heart instructing him as the arena of that guidance. No seat is recorded (104 none): the blessing is not seated in an organ but is the whole grateful person turning to God; no source (103), manner, intensity, effect or prohibition is logged. The effect-silence reads as devotion offered for its own sake. The lens stays on the inner being: the movement is the self's answering thanks, and its locus is named an interior state (116).
narratives.variation_note: This is barak directed at God in thanks, not the esher-state; and among the bless-God readings this one is narrowly occasioned — blessing specifically for divine counsel/guidance, not for rescue, hearing, or in the assembly.

narratives.narrative: As the psalm recounts a great deliverance, praise erupts: 'the LORD lives, and blessed be my rock' (101 doxology; 102 affect). The self (105) blesses the living God — its rock and the God of its salvation (106) — the act a doxology (107) coupled to that title 'my rock' (112 bless-my-rock). The blessing is the interior breaking open as the rescue is told; God and the subdued nations are the arena, but the movement narrated is the man's own upsurge of praise. Nothing is seated in an organ (104 none), and source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are all silent — the doxology is unqualified and terminal, praise that goes nowhere beyond itself. Its locus is an inner state (116): the whole recounting turns, from within, to ascribing greatness to the deliverer.
narratives.variation_note: Among the bless-God (barak) doxologies this one is triggered by military deliverance and the title 'my rock / God of my salvation'; its locus is logged internal:ib-state rather than external:god, framing it as the interior's own eruption more than a directed cultic act.

narratives.narrative: The vindicated interior, having pleaded its integrity through the whole psalm, closes by turning to public praise: 'in the great assembly I will bless the LORD' (101; 102 affect). Standing now on level ground, the self (105) performs the blessing (106) as a doxology (107) coupled to the assembly (112 bless-in-assembly) — the private drama of integrity resolving into corporate worship, the congregation its arena. No seat is named (104 none): this is not organ-located but the whole steadied person; source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are absent. The effect-silence tells: the blessing is where the movement ends, the psalm's destination, not a means to something further. Locus is interior (116) — the vindication felt within issues in the act of blessing God among others.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct from the other bless-God readings by its setting: this blessing is explicitly public, resolved 'in the great assembly', the endpoint of a plea for vindication rather than gratitude for a specific rescue or counsel.

narratives.narrative: The psalm opens dreading God's silence (v1, 'lest you be silent to me'); at v6 the feared silence has not come, and the interior reverses into blessing: 'blessed be the LORD, for he has heard' (101; 102 affect). The self (105) blesses God (106) in gratitude-for-hearing (107), the act coupled to the very fact that he heard the voice of the pleas (112 bless-he-heard). The whole movement is a turn — dread of unanswered prayer flipping into thanks — with God as the arena that did not stay deaf. Nothing is seated (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect, prohibition are all silent, so the blessing is unqualified and self-contained. Locus is internal (116): the reversal happens inside the man, fear giving way to blessing.
narratives.variation_note: Set apart from sibling bless-God readings by its trigger — gratitude specifically that the dreaded divine silence was broken and the plea heard; it is the hinge that turns the psalm's fear into praise.

narratives.narrative: Out of a long lament of siege, reproach and terror on every side, the interior marvels: 'blessed be the LORD, for he has wondrously shown his steadfast love to me' (101; 102 affect). The self (105) blesses God (106) in grateful-blessing (107) that names the deliverance a wonder, coupled to that wondrous love in a besieged city (112 bless-wondrous-love). The movement is astonishment turning to praise — the beleaguered inner being awed that chesed reached it in extremity, God's shelter its arena. No seat (104 none), and source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are unrecorded: the marvel is not organ-lodged, not graded, and goes nowhere beyond the blessing itself. Locus is interior (116): the wonder is felt within and voiced as blessing.
narratives.variation_note: Among the bless-God readings this one is coloured by marvel — blessing that explicitly names the rescue 'wondrous', arising from the extremity of siege and reproach rather than routine gratitude.

narratives.narrative: This beatitude locates human happiness not in innocence but in pardon: 'blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered' (101; 102 affect). The bearer is the forgiven one (105), and the operation is the interior pronouncing itself happy precisely there (106) — a beatitude-of-pardon (107) coupled to the state of being forgiven (112 blessed-forgiven). The psalm's own middle (the wasting bones of unconfessed sin, the relief of confession) shows the felt weight this blessedness answers; the movement is the interior's release once guilt is lifted. No seat is named (104 none) — the happiness is not organ-located; source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent, marking it unqualified and terminal. Locus is an inner state (116): blessedness as the settled relief of the pardoned.
narratives.variation_note: An esher-beatitude (a state), unlike the barak bless-God readings; and within the esher group it is distinctive for grounding happiness in forgiveness/pardon rather than in fearing God, trust, or discipline.

narratives.narrative: 'I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth' (101; 102 affect) makes blessing not an event but a standing posture. The self (105) resolves to the operation of unbroken praise (106), a continual-praise (107) coupled to its very ceaselessness (112 bless-at-all-times) — a commitment stretched across all times, the delivered life its arena. No seat is recorded (104 none): though the mouth voices it, the study logs no organ-seat, reading the blessing as the whole person's fixed orientation; source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The absence of any effect marks the praise as its own end, a way of being rather than a means. Locus is interior (116): the resolve is an inner stance turned continually Godward.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct among bless-God readings by its temporal reach: not a single occasioned blessing but a vow of unceasing, 'at all times' praise — blessing made the constant posture of a whole life.

narratives.narrative: Within the wisdom portrait of the righteous, the interior's disposition shows as habit: 'he is ever lending generously, and his children become a blessing' (101; 102 volition — this is a bent of the will, not a feeling). The bearer is the righteous man (105), and the operation is sustained, ongoing generosity (106), a habitual-generosity (107) coupled to its very continuousness (112 ever-lending) — the poor and needy the arena toward which the open-handed will moves. No seat is named (104 none): generosity here is not organ-lodged but a settled orientation of the whole person; source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are all silent. That the will-type is flagged (volition) while affect-language is absent is itself the finding — this reading watches the inner being as a disposition that acts, its outflow blessing even the next generation. Locus is an inner state (116).

'Blessed is the man who makes the LORD his trust, who does not turn to the proud, to those who go astray after a lie' (101; 102 affect) weighs an interior by the direction of its reliance. The bearer is the trusting man (105); the operation pronounces him happy for rightly-placed trust (106/107) — leaning on God rather than on proud liars — coupled to that trust itself (112 blessed-who-trusts). The beatitude is defined as much by a refusal (not turning to the proud) as by a leaning, yet no prohibition row is logged (113 absent): the turning-away is described, not forbidden. No seat (104 none), and source, manner, intensity and effect are silent — an unqualified, terminal happiness. Locus is interior (116): blessedness as the settled state of an inner being that has chosen where to lean.
narratives.variation_note: An esher state-beatitude; among the esher readings it is marked by its object — happiness grounded specifically in trust rightly placed (and refusing the proud), rather than in forgiveness, discipline, or the fear of God.

narratives.narrative: The doxology sealing Book I lifts God above the whole span of time: 'blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting' (101; 102 affect). The self (105) blesses God (106) in a doxology (107) coupled to that everlasting reach (112 bless-everlasting). Rising straight out of a psalm of sickness, betrayal and malicious enemies, the movement is the interior refusing to end in complaint, turning instead to endless blessing — God the arena over all time. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent, so the blessing is unqualified and terminal. Locus is interior (116): the man's own inward turn to bless.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct from sibling bless-God doxologies by its liturgical function and horizon — a Book-sealing 'from everlasting to everlasting' blessing that rises out of a lament of betrayal, its reach the whole span of time rather than a single occasion.

narratives.narrative: This is the dark inversion of blessing, and it must be read at full weight: 'while he lives, he counts himself blessed' (101; 102 action). Here the bearer is the rich man (105), and the operation is barak turned reflexive — to count blessed (106) — with the target his own soul (107 himself), coupled to the self (112 'of the self'). Blessing, which everywhere else moves toward God, here curves back onto the self in smug self-congratulation; the discovery marks it the self-satisfaction that death will silence, for the man in his pomp is like the beasts that perish. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent — the study neither condemns nor grades it with a prohibition row, letting the passage's own verdict (v20) stand. Locus is interior (116): the movement is wholly inward, a soul blessing itself. The absence of any effect is telling — this blessing produces nothing that outlasts the grave.
narratives.variation_note: The one descent-reading among the bless (barak) entries: the operation is reflexive (self-directed) rather than Godward, its target the man's own soul and its coupling 'of the self' — the smug interior, not worship, marking a full ascent-to-descent shift from every other bless-God reading.

narratives.narrative: A second dark reading exposes blessing split from the heart: 'they bless with their mouths, but inwardly they curse' (101; 102 action). Here alone a seat is named — the mouth (104) — and the bearer is the enemies (105), whose operation is an outward blessing (106) directed with their mouths while cursing within, the target set precisely against that inward curse (107; 112 the paired split). The manner is explicit: outwardly, hypocritically (108). The finding is the fracture of the false interior — mouth and heart at war, the very portrait of the betrayer — plotting to thrust the victim down while taking pleasure in falsehood. Source, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent; the study does not moralise with a prohibition row but lets the split stand as evidence. Locus is interior (116): the true drama is inside, the divorce of speech from what the heart actually holds.
narratives.variation_note: The sole reading where blessing is hypocritical: uniquely it records a seat (the mouth) and an explicit manner (outwardly, hypocritically), and the operation is set against an inward curse — blessing as mask rather than worship, the inverse of every sincere bless-God reading.

narratives.narrative: 'So I will bless you as long as I live; in your name I will lift up my hands' (101; 102 action) makes blessing the constant business of a whole life. The self (105) blesses God (106), the target God in his name (107), with an explicit manner — as long as he lives, hands lifted (108) — and a coupling that the blessing is expressed in the very lifting of the hands (112). Out of a dry and weary land where the soul thirsts, the movement is lifelong devotion, God the arena the interior clings to. No seat (104 none); source, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent — the blessing is not organ-lodged and produces no further logged outcome, worship offered for its own sake. Uniquely here the locus is external:god (116): the reading tilts the movement outward, toward God, rather than resting in an inner state.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive among bless-God readings for its embodied, lifelong manner (uplifted hands, 'as long as I live') and, notably, for a locus flagged external:god rather than internal — the movement read as directed worship rather than an interior condition.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed is the one you choose and bring near, to dwell in your courts' (101; 102 status) locates the deepest human happiness in nearness to God. The bearer is the one God chooses (105); the operation is to be blessed / brought near (106), with the manner spelled out — chosen, drawn near to dwell in God's courts (108) — and the coupling that this issues in being satisfied with God's goodness (112). Notably the target is 'none' (107): the blessedness is not aimed at a further object; it terminates in the nearness itself. No seat (104 none); source, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The locus here is external:god (116) — the happiness is read as constituted by the relation to God, not merely an inner glow. The absence of a target, paired with satisfaction as the coupling, is the finding: election-to-nearness is its own fulfilment.
narratives.variation_note: Among the esher-beatitudes this one is unusual in three logged ways — its type is 'status' (a granted standing), its target is explicitly 'none' (nearness is the end), and its locus is external:god; happiness here is election and drawing-near, not a disposition the person generates.

narratives.narrative: 'Bless our God, O peoples' (101; 102 action) widens blessing to a corporate summons. The bearer is the peoples (105), called to the operation of blessing (106) with our God as target (107), the manner being to make the sound of his praise heard, coupled with that resounding praise (108/112). The ground, in the passage, is the God who kept their soul among the living and did not let their feet slip through severe testing — so gratitude is voiced outward as blessing, all the earth its arena. No seat (104 none); source, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent — an unqualified summons. Locus is external:god (116): the movement is turned outward in shared worship. The finding is that the interior life of blessing is here made plural and public, an audible summons rather than a private stirring.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct among bless-God readings for being a corporate, imperative summons to 'the peoples' with an audible manner (making his praise heard), grounded in communal preservation through testing rather than an individual's occasion.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed be God, because he has not rejected my prayer or removed his steadfast love from me' (101; 102 action) is a rare reading that records its source. Uniquely, source is present (103): the blessing arises because God has not removed his chesed. The bearer is the psalmist (105), the operation blessing (106) with God as target (107), the manner 'for not rejecting his prayer nor removing his love' (108), grounded/coupled in the accepted prayer (112). The movement is fully traced here — a named cause (kept love) producing the interior's blessing — the psalm ending as it began, in blessing. No seat (104 none); intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is external:god (116). That this reading, unlike most, carries an explicit source is the finding: the blessing is shown flowing from a specific divine constancy.
narratives.variation_note: One of a small cluster of bless-God readings (with Ps 68:19, 26, 35) that record an explicit source — here God's unremoved steadfast love and accepted prayer; distinct from the many source-silent doxologies in that the cause of the blessing is named.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed be the LORD, who daily bears us up; God is our salvation' (101; 102 action) blesses God for a day-by-day sustaining. Source is present here (103): the blessing is because God daily carries them, the God of salvation. The bearer is the worshippers (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the Lord who bears them up (107), the manner 'daily' (108), coupled to God-our-salvation who bears us up (112). Set amid a hymn of the mighty warrior-God riding the heavens, the finding is that the same God is the everyday burden-bearer of his people — power and tenderness held together. No seat (104 none); intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is external:god (116): worship directed outward. The named source and the 'daily' manner together trace the full movement from cause to blessing.
narratives.variation_note: Within the source-bearing bless-God cluster, this reading is marked by its 'daily' manner and its source in God's continual bearing-up — the routine, day-by-day sustaining, set against the martial imagery, rather than a single dramatic rescue.

narratives.narrative: 'Bless God in the great congregation, the LORD, O you who are of Israel's fountain' (101; 102 action) is the corporate summons within the festal procession. Source is present (103): of the God who has worked and summoned his power for them (v28). The bearer is the great congregation (105); the operation is blessing (106), the target God in the congregation (107), the manner 'in the great congregation' (108), the coupling the corporate blessing led by the singers (112). The movement is public, choreographed worship — tribes in procession, singers and musicians — the assembly its arena. No seat (104 none); intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is external:god (116). The finding: the interior act of blessing is here wholly socialised, a summons voiced in and by the gathered people.
narratives.variation_note: A bless-God summons distinguished by its liturgical setting — the great congregation and festal procession, led by the singers — with a named source (God's power worked for them); corporate and processional rather than an individual's private blessing.

narratives.narrative: The war-hymn's closing doxology: 'he is the one who gives power and strength to his people. Blessed be God!' (101; 102 action). Source is present (103): the God who gives power and strength to his people. The bearer is the worshippers (105), the operation blessing (106), the target God who strengthens his people (107), and the coupling notes this closing blessing echoing v19 and v26 (112). The movement is the whole hymn resolving, as it has three times, into blessing — the awesome God of the sanctuary honoured for empowering his own. No seat (104 none); manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is external:god (116). The finding is structural: blessing is the recurring landing-place of this psalm's interior, God's strengthening of the people the named cause.
narratives.variation_note: The third of Psalm 68's bless-God readings and its closing seal (coupled explicitly to v19 and v26); it differs by naming God's gift of 'power and strength to his people' as its source and by functioning as the hymn's final resolution rather than an interior summons.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things' (101; 102 action) is the doxology closing Book II. The bearer is the worshippers (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD who alone works wonders (107), coupled with the parallel blessing of his glorious name in v19 (112). Rising from a royal psalm's prayer for the king, the movement lifts from the earthly king to the King of kings — the sole wonder-worker its object. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent, an unqualified doxology. Locus is external:god (116). The finding is the ascent of scale: the interior's blessing widens from the king's reign to the God who alone does wondrous things.
narratives.variation_note: Paired with #10 in the same closing doxology; this half blesses the LORD 'who alone does wondrous things', where #10 blesses his glorious name — the distinction is object (the God himself vs. his name) and the outward-reaching longing that his glory fill the earth belongs to #10.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed be his glorious name forever; may the whole earth be filled with his glory' (101; 102 action) is the great Amen ending Book II. The bearer is the worshippers (105), the operation blessing (106), the target God's glorious name forever (107), the manner 'forever, the whole earth filled with his glory' (108), coupled to the blessing of the LORD who does wonders in v18 (112). The movement reaches its widest horizon — blessing of the name paired with the longing that his glory fill all the earth, the whole creation its arena. No seat (104 none); source, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is external:god (116). The finding is expansiveness: the interior's blessing does not rest content but stretches toward a world-filling glory.
narratives.variation_note: The companion of #18: same doxology, but this reading blesses God's *name* (not God directly) and carries the distinctive world-wide manner — 'forever, the whole earth filled with his glory' — pushing the blessing to its broadest horizon.

narratives.narrative: The pilgrim psalm's closing beatitude rests happiness wholly on trust: 'blessed is the one who trusts in you' (101; 102 state). The bearer is the one who trusts God (105); the operation is to be blessed (106), the target being in the trusting of God (107), coupled to that trust (112). After a psalm of longing for the courts and going 'from strength to strength', the movement settles all blessedness onto reliance on the LORD of hosts. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent — an unqualified, terminal state. Locus is interior (116): blessedness as the settled inner condition of the trusting person. The finding is concentration — the whole rich psalm distilled to trust as the single ground of happiness.
narratives.variation_note: One of three esher-beatitudes in Psalm 84 (with v4, v5); this one grounds happiness in *trust* and closes the psalm, where v4 grounds it in dwelling in God's house and v5 in having one's strength in God — three different footings for the same blessed state.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed are those who dwell in your house, ever singing your praise' (101; 102 state) makes happiness a matter of abiding presence. The bearer is those who dwell in God's house (105); the operation is to be blessed (106) in God's presence (107), coupled to their ceaseless praise (112). The passage's longing soul, fainting for the courts and envying even the sparrow's nest at the altar, shows the desire this blessedness answers — nearness sustained. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116): blessedness as the inner state of those who abide with God. The finding is that happiness is here located in dwelling — a settled proximity that overflows in unending praise.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct from Psalm 84's other beatitudes by its footing: happiness in *dwelling* in God's house (coupled with ceaseless praise), where v5 grounds it in God-given strength and v12 in trust.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed are those whose strength is in you, in whose heart are the highways to Zion' (101; 102 state) names the happiness of the God-reliant pilgrim. The bearer is those whose strength is in God (105); the operation is to be blessed (106) in reliance on God (107), coupled to the highways to Zion in the heart (112). The movement is the pilgrim whose power is not his own, who turns the Valley of Baca into springs and goes from strength to strength — God the source of a strength the self lacks. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116): blessedness as the inner condition of the God-strengthened. The finding is dependence — happiness for the one whose strength is confessedly borrowed.
narratives.variation_note: Among Psalm 84's beatitudes this one grounds happiness in *God-given strength* and the inward pilgrim road ('highways to Zion in the heart'), distinct from the dwelling-footing of v4 and the trust-footing of v12.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed are the people who know the festal shout, who walk, O LORD, in the light of your face' (101; 102 state) sets happiness in worship of God as king. The bearer is the people (105); the operation is to be blessed (106), the target those who know the festal shout (107), coupled — the row reads — to knowing the shout and walking in the light of God's face (112). The passage's foundation is God's throne of righteousness and justice, chesed and faithfulness going before him; the movement is a people's blessedness in acclaiming him. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is corporate and cultic: this blessed state belongs to a people that knows how to shout God's kingship and walk in his favour.
narratives.variation_note: An esher state-beatitude whose bearer is a *people* (corporate) and whose footing is knowing the festal shout / walking in God's face — worship-of-the-king, distinct from the individual, disposition-based beatitudes (trust, discipline, fear).

narratives.narrative: Out of the Psalter's bleakest covenant-lament — a rejected king, a defiled crown, wrath burning like fire — the interior still seals the book in blessing: 'blessed be the LORD forever' (101; 102 action). The bearer is the psalmist and all (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD forever (107), the coupling read as the everlasting doxology (112). The movement is striking: blessing wrung *out of* lament, the crushed interior refusing to end in complaint. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent — an unqualified doxology. Locus, oddly logged, points to the everlasting doxology itself (116). The finding, read without flinching, is that blessing here does not answer to circumstance: the psalm's anguish is unresolved, yet the interior blesses anyway.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct among bless-God doxologies for its context — it rises directly out of unresolved covenant-lament (the rejected anointed), making it blessing offered against the grain of felt experience rather than in response to rescue.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O LORD, and whom you teach out of your law' (101; 102 state) is the hard-edged beatitude that reads chastening as grace. The bearer is the disciplined man (105); the operation is to be blessed (106) under God's discipline (107), coupled to being taught God's law (112). In a psalm that cries out against wicked rulers and the near-slipping foot, the movement finds happiness precisely in being corrected — discipline the arena of a deeper rest 'from days of trouble'. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116). The finding, uncomfortable but plainly supported, is that blessedness can be located in being disciplined — the inner being counts God's correction, not its absence, as its good.
narratives.variation_note: Among the esher-beatitudes this one is distinctive and countervalent: happiness grounded in *being disciplined and taught* by God — chastening read as blessing — rather than in trust, forgiveness, or flourishing.

narratives.narrative: 'Sing to the LORD, bless his name; tell of his salvation from day to day' (101; 102 action) folds blessing into a global summons to praise. The bearer is all the earth (105), the operation blessing (106), the target God's name (107), coupled with the singing that surrounds it (112 paired with singing). The movement is adoration of the name — praise as blessing — spread to all peoples, God's glory declared among the nations its arena. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent, an unqualified summons. Locus is logged as paired with singing (116). The finding is that here blessing is one facet of a wider act of praise: to bless the name is to sing and to tell his salvation daily.
narratives.variation_note: A bless-God-name summons directed to 'all the earth' and set inside the call to sing and declare his salvation among the nations — distinct from the individual soul-summons of Psalm 103 by its universal scope.

narratives.narrative: 'Enter his gates with thanksgiving... give thanks to him; bless his name' (101; 102 action) makes blessing part of the approach to worship. The bearer is the worshippers (105), the operation blessing (106), the target God's name (107), coupled with giving thanks (112). The passage grounds it in God's goodness and his steadfast love enduring forever; the movement is the gathered people entering the courts and, as they come, blessing the name. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is logged as paired with giving thanks (116). The finding is that blessing here is liturgical motion — the act of entering God's presence with thanks, of which blessing his name is the crown.
narratives.variation_note: A bless-God-name summons framed by temple-entry and thanksgiving; distinct from Psalm 96's world-wide call by its cultic setting (entering the gates and courts) rather than declaring among the nations.

narratives.narrative: 'Bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name' (101; 102 action) turns the summons inward: the self commands itself to praise. The bearer is the psalmist (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD / his holy name (107), coupled outward to God (112) and logged as the soul stirred to bless (116). The movement is a self-address — the whole person, 'all that is within me', roused to bless — the litany of benefits (forgiving, healing, redeeming, crowning) its ground. No seat (104 none): though 'all within' is invoked rhetorically, no single organ-seat is recorded; source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is the reflexive structure — blessing begins by the interior summoning itself, praise as an act of self-command.
narratives.variation_note: The first of Psalm 103's self-summons pair (with v2): distinctive for addressing the soul and 'all that is within me' to bless God's *holy name* at the psalm's opening — the reflexive stirring-up of the whole interior.

narratives.narrative: 'Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits' (101; 102 action) renews the self-exhortation and ties it to memory. The bearer is the psalmist (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD (107), coupled to God (112) and paired with not forgetting his benefits (116). The movement is the resolve to praise reinforced by remembering — blessing bound to the refusal to forget forgiveness, healing and redemption. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding sits in the coupling: here blessing is guarded by memory — the interior blesses by holding on to what God has done, so that gratitude is a discipline against forgetfulness.
narratives.variation_note: The repeated self-summons of Psalm 103, distinguished from v1 by its coupling to *memory* — 'forget not all his benefits' — where v1 stirs the whole inner being and v22 closes the frame.

narratives.narrative: 'Bless the LORD, O my soul' (101; 102 action) returns at the psalm's end, sealing it as it began. The bearer is the psalmist (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD (107), coupled to God (112) and paired with the soul (116). After summoning angels, hosts and all his works to bless, the interior comes back to itself — the self once more the first and last voice of praise. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is the closing return: the cosmic call to bless resolves back into the single soul commanding itself, blessing framed as an inner act that opens and closes the whole.
narratives.variation_note: The closing bracket of Psalm 103's self-summons (matching v1, v2): distinct in function — it seals the psalm after the universe has been called to bless, the interior returning to command itself once more.

narratives.narrative: 'Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, you are very great' (101; 102 action) opens the creation-hymn with the self summoning itself. The bearer is the psalmist (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD (107), coupled to God (112) and paired with the soul, bookended at v35 (116). The whole catalogue that follows — the clouds his chariot, the waters fleeing at his rebuke, the mountains and valleys set in place — is the ground of this blessing; the movement is the interior stirring itself to bless the great Creator. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is anticipatory: the blessing is stated first and then *earned* by the survey of creation that follows, an inner resolve the psalm proceeds to justify.
narratives.variation_note: The opening half of Psalm 104's frame (bookended with v35): distinct from Psalm 103's self-summons by its object — blessing God the *Creator*, with the whole creation-catalogue as its warrant — and by being the frame's opening rather than close.

narratives.narrative: 'Bless the LORD, O my soul! Praise the LORD!' (101; 102 action) closes the creation-hymn, the soul returning to bless after surveying all God's works. The bearer is the psalmist (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD (107), coupled to God (112) and logged as the bookend to the opening blessing of v1 (116). Notably the close comes right after 'let sinners be consumed from the earth' — the blessing of God held together with a longing that evil be no more, which the reading does not soften. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is the completed frame: the interior, having contemplated the Creator's works, comes home to bless — praise as the movement's destination.
narratives.variation_note: The closing half of Psalm 104's frame (bookend to v1): distinct in placement and in its immediate context — it follows the wish that sinners be consumed, so the soul's blessing here is voiced alongside a call for evil's end rather than at the hymn's fresh opening.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed are they who observe justice, who do righteousness at all times' (101; 102 state) is the beatitude set before a national confession. The bearer is those who keep justice (105); the operation is to be blessed (106) in keeping justice (107), coupled to that inner state (112) and paired with observing justice and doing righteousness (116). Placed just before the fathers' rebellion is confessed, the movement holds up sustained righteousness as the standard the fathers failed — happiness for the interior that does justice 'at all times'. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116). The finding is the rhetorical placement: the blessed state is named as a foil, the ideal against which the confession of sin is measured.
narratives.variation_note: Among the esher-beatitudes this one grounds happiness in *doing justice and righteousness continually* and functions as a foil to communal sin — distinct from the God-fearing, trusting, or disciplined footings of the other esher readings.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting' (101; 102 action) is the doxology closing Book IV. The bearer is the worshippers (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD, the God of Israel (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with the closing praise (116). It rises out of a long confession of rebellion, idolatry, even child-sacrifice, and God's repeated relenting; the movement is the community, having rehearsed its own faithlessness and God's mercy, blessing him across all time. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is the same as elsewhere in the book-seams — blessing wrung from a history of failure, praise the appointed endpoint even after confession.
narratives.variation_note: A Book-sealing 'everlasting to everlasting' doxology like those closing Books I, II and III; this one is distinctive for rising out of a searching national confession of idolatry and rebellion rather than out of rescue or a royal prayer.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in his commandments' (101; 102 state) is the beatitude the whole psalm unfolds. The bearer is the God-fearing man (105); the operation is to be blessed (106) in fearing God (107), coupled to that inner state (112) and paired with fearing God and delighting in his commandments (116). The psalm then traces what this happiness looks like — a firm, unafraid heart, generosity, light in darkness — but the root is the fear of God joined to delight in his law. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116). The finding is that the blessed state here is defined by a paradoxical pairing — reverent fear *and* delight — as the interior's settled orientation.
narratives.variation_note: An esher-beatitude grounded in the *fear of the LORD joined to delight in his commandments*; it heads the psalm as the state the rest describes, distinct from the trust, discipline, or justice footings of the other esher readings.

narratives.narrative: 'His offspring will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed' (101; 102 state, but barak) extends blessing beyond the man to his line. The bearer is the upright (105); the operation is to be blessed (106) by God (107), coupled to the inner state (112) and paired with the upright (116). Within the portrait of the God-fearer, the movement is generational — the blessing resting on the upright and their offspring, mightiness in the land its sign. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is scope: whereas v1's esher names the man's own happiness, this barak-reading shows the blessing as something *conferred* that reaches his descendants — a blessedness that outlasts the individual.
narratives.variation_note: In the same psalm as the v1 esher-beatitude, this reading uses barak and shifts the bearer outward to the *offspring / generation of the upright* — blessing as conferred and inherited, not the man's own felt state.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and forevermore' (101; 102 action) blesses God's name across all time. The bearer is the worshippers (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the name of the LORD (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with praising his name (116). Set in a hymn of the God who is high above the nations yet stoops to raise the poor from the dust, the movement is the servants of the LORD blessing his name from sunrise to sunset, everywhere and always. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is the temporal and spatial totality — blessing the name 'from this time forth and forevermore', from the rising of the sun to its setting.
narratives.variation_note: A bless-God's-name reading distinguished by its all-encompassing temporal reach ('from this time forth and forevermore', sunrise to sunset), voiced by the LORD's servants — distinct from the occasioned or entry-liturgy name-blessings.

narratives.narrative: 'But we will bless the LORD from this time forth and forevermore' (101; 102 action) sets the living's endless worship against the silence of the dead. The bearer is 'we', the living (105); the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD forevermore (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with the closing praise (116). The passage's contrast is stark — 'the dead do not praise the LORD, nor any who go down into silence' — so the movement is life itself claimed as the time for blessing, the interior seizing its breath to praise while it can. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding, read at full weight, is that blessing is bound to the living: the descent into silence ends it, and so the interior blesses now and 'forevermore' against that dark backdrop.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct among bless-God readings for being defined against death — 'the dead do not praise' — so this blessing is the living's deliberate claim on the time they have, rather than an occasioned thanksgiving or summons.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD' (101; 102 action) is the processional welcome pronounced over the one entering. The bearer is the worshippers (105), the operation to bless / pronounce blessed (106), the target him who comes in the LORD's name (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with blessing from the house of the LORD (116). Amid a psalm of marvel ('this is the LORD's doing') and the cry 'save us', the movement is a benediction over an arriving worshipper — blessing directed manward but in God's name. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding, notably, is directional: here the human interior blesses *another human* who comes in God's name, not God directly — a benediction at the threshold.
narratives.variation_note: One of two blessings at Psalm 118:26; this reading blesses the *one who comes* (a human, in God's name) — a benediction directed manward — where its companion #16 is the answering blessing spoken back from the temple.

narratives.narrative: 'We bless you from the house of the LORD' (101; 102 action) is the answering blessing spoken from the temple over the coming worshippers. The bearer is the priests / worshippers (105), the operation blessing (106), the target 'from the house of the LORD' (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with the entering blessed (116). The movement completes an exchange: the arriving one is blessed (v26a), and the sanctuary blesses back — a two-way benediction at the gate. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is relational reciprocity: the interior life of blessing here is a mutual act, temple and pilgrim blessing one another, blessing flowing both directions in God's name.
narratives.variation_note: The companion of #15 in the same verse: this reading is the blessing spoken *from the house of the LORD* back over the entrants — the answering, reciprocal half of the threshold exchange, distinct from #15's blessing of the one who comes.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the LORD' (101; 102 state) opens the great law-psalm. The bearer is the blameless (105); the operation is to be blessed (106), and here the target is 'none' (107) — the blessedness is not aimed beyond itself — coupled within its char-arc across the psalm (112) and located as an inner state (116). The movement is the whole life of Torah-keeping pronounced happy at the threshold, the psalm's 1000-fold meditation on the law its unfolding. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding sits in the 'none' target: this blessedness terminates in the blameless walk itself — happiness is the wholeness of a life shaped by God's word, not a reward pointed elsewhere.
narratives.variation_note: An esher-beatitude opening Psalm 119, grounded in the *blameless way / walking in the law*; distinctive for its 'none' target (blessedness terminal in the walk itself), paired with the v2 beatitude on the whole-hearted keepers.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed are you, O LORD; teach me your statutes' (101; 102 action) turns, mid-psalm, from beatitude to blessing God directly. The bearer is the psalmist (105), the operation to bless God (106), the target God's word (107), coupled within its char-arc across the psalm (112) and located external:god (116). Strikingly, the blessing is fused with a petition — the interior blesses God in the very breath it asks to be taught his statutes, the stored-up word in the heart (v11) its context. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is the coupling of praise and petition: here to bless God is also to ask of him, worship and learning held in one movement of the inner being.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct from Psalm 119's esher-beatitudes (v1, v2) by being a barak addressed *to God* and fused with a petition ('teach me your statutes') — blessing that is simultaneously a request, its locus external:god rather than an inner state.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed are those who keep his testimonies, who seek him with their whole heart' (101; 102 state) is the second opening beatitude of the law-psalm. The bearer is those who keep (105); the operation is to be blessed (106), the target again 'none' (107) — terminal in the keeping — coupled within its char-arc across the psalm (112) and located as an inner state (116). The movement adds whole-heartedness to blamelessness: happiness for those who not only walk rightly but seek God with the entire heart. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding, paired with v1, is intensification — blessedness deepened from an outward blameless way to an inward, whole-hearted seeking.
narratives.variation_note: The companion to the v1 beatitude: same esher-state, but this reading adds *whole-hearted seeking* to keeping the testimonies — an inward intensification beyond v1's blameless walk; both share the terminal 'none' target.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth' (101; 102 action) blesses God at the recognition of a devouring just escaped. The bearer is the people (105), the operation to bless God (106), the target God for not making them prey (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with escaping the teeth (116). The whole psalm imagines the alternative — swallowed alive, swept away by the flood, torn by teeth — 'if it had not been the LORD who was on our side'; the movement is corporate gratitude at deliverance from being consumed. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is that blessing here springs from a vividly imagined near-death — the interior blessing God precisely by seeing what it was spared.
narratives.variation_note: A bless-God reading occasioned by escape from near-destruction (the flood, the teeth), voiced corporately ('us'); distinct from the general doxologies by resting on a specific, vividly pictured deliverance from being devoured.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed is the man who fills his quiver with them' (101; 102 state) locates happiness in a house full of children. The bearer is the man with children (105); the operation is to be blessed (106) with a full quiver (107), coupled to the inner state (112) and paired with not being put to shame at the gate (116). The passage first insists children are 'a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward,' so the movement grounds the man's happiness in a divine gift — strength and standing among enemies flowing from offspring. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116). The finding is that this blessedness is concrete and social — a full quiver, a man unashamed in the gate — happiness embodied in family and public standing.
narratives.variation_note: Among the esher-beatitudes this one is distinctive for its concrete, this-worldly footing — happiness in *children / a full quiver* (God's gift) and public standing at the gate — rather than in an interior disposition like trust or fear.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in his ways' (101; 102 state) opens the pilgrim psalm with the fear of God as the root of happiness. The bearer is the God-fearer (105); the operation is to be blessed (106) in fearing God (107), coupled to the inner state (112) and paired with fearing and walking (116). The movement joins reverence to conduct — happiness for the one whose fear of God shapes his walk — which the next line unfolds as eating the fruit of one's labour. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116). The finding is the familiar wisdom footing — the fear of the LORD as the ground of a blessed life — here opening a psalm of ordinary flourishing.
narratives.variation_note: One of two esher-beatitudes framing Psalm 128 (with v2); this one names the *state* — happiness in fearing the LORD and walking his ways — where v2 turns to the realized *experience* of that blessedness (eating one's labour's fruit).

narratives.narrative: 'You shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands; you shall be blessed, and it shall be well with you' (101; 102 state) turns the opening beatitude into lived experience. The bearer is the God-fearer (105); the operation is to be blessed (106), the target eating his labour's fruit (107), coupled to the inner state (112) and paired with it being well with him (116). The movement is realization — the blessedness named in v1 now tasted in ordinary satisfactions, work that yields its fruit and a settled well-being. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116). The finding is the shift from ascription to enjoyment: blessedness here is not merely pronounced but experienced as the fruit of one's own hands.
narratives.variation_note: The companion of v1: same esher-state, but this reading is the *realized enjoyment* of blessedness — eating one's labour's fruit, 'it shall be well with you' — where v1 names the God-fearing condition; the difference is pronouncement vs. lived experience.

narratives.narrative: 'Thus shall the man be blessed who fears the LORD' (101; 102 state, barak) is the summary pronouncement of the psalm. The bearer is the God-fearer (105); the operation is to be blessed (106) for fearing God (107), coupled to the inner state (112) and paired with fearing the LORD (116). Following the two esher-beatitudes, this barak-reading gathers them into a verdict — the God-fearer *is* the blessed man — and turns immediately to a conferred blessing 'from Zion'. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116). The finding is summative and shifts from state to conferral: where the esher lines describe the happiness, this barak line pronounces and confers it, blessing spoken over the man.
narratives.variation_note: In the same psalm as the v1/v2 esher-beatitudes, this reading uses barak to *pronounce and confer* the blessing on the God-fearer ('thus shall the man be blessed'), then opens to blessing 'from Zion' — a shift from describing the state to conferring it.

narratives.narrative: 'Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD, who stand by night in the house of the LORD' (101; 102 action) summons the temple-servants to night-worship. The bearer is the servants (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD by night (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with lifting the hands (116). The movement is nocturnal — those who keep watch through the dark hours called to fill them with blessing, the house of the LORD its arena. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is temporal and vocational: blessing here is the work of the night-watch, the interior turned to praise precisely in the hours when others sleep.
narratives.variation_note: A bless-God summons distinctive for its setting — the *night-watch* of the temple-servants ('who stand by night') — distinct from daytime or festal blessing; paired with v2's repeated call.

narratives.narrative: 'Lift up your hands to the holy place and bless the LORD' (101; 102 action) presses the summons home with a bodily gesture. The bearer is the servants (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with the lifted hands (116). The movement joins inner blessing to outward posture — hands raised toward the sanctuary as the interior blesses — worship made visible in the night. No seat (104 none): the hands are the gesture of blessing, but no organ-seat is logged; source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is embodiment: blessing here is not only voiced but enacted with the body, the repeated call driving the servants from resolve to gesture.
narratives.variation_note: The repeated call of Psalm 134 (with v1): distinct in adding the *bodily gesture* — lifting the hands toward the holy place — where v1 issues the summons to the night-standing servants; the difference is the move from call to embodied act.

narratives.narrative: 'O house of Israel, bless the LORD!' (101; 102 action) is the first of a fourfold summons, and it stands against the preceding portrait of dead idols with ears that cannot hear and no breath in their mouths. The bearer is the house of Israel (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with the fourfold blessing (116). The movement sets living worship over against lifeless idols — 'those who make them become like them' — the whole nation summoned to bless the true, breathing God. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is the contrast: blessing is the mark of the living God's people, the opposite of the mute idol and its mute makers.
narratives.variation_note: The first of Psalm 135's fourfold summons; addressed to the *house of Israel* (the whole nation) and set pointedly against the mute idols — distinct from the Aaron, Levi and God-fearer calls that follow (#19, #20, #21).

narratives.narrative: 'O house of Aaron, bless the LORD!' (101; 102 action) is the second summons of the fourfold call, addressed to the priests. The bearer is the house of Aaron (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with the fourfold blessing (116). Following the call to all Israel, the movement narrows to the priestly line — those whose office is worship summoned to bless, still against the backdrop of the breathless idols. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is the widening liturgical structure: blessing is distributed across the orders of Israel, each in turn called by name to the same act.
narratives.variation_note: The second call of the fourfold summons, addressed specifically to the *house of Aaron* (the priests) — distinct from the whole-nation call of #18 and the Levite/God-fearer calls of #20/#21; same act, different order of Israel named.

narratives.narrative: 'O house of Levi, bless the LORD!' (101; 102 action) is the third summons, addressed to the Levites. The bearer is the house of Levi (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with the fourfold blessing (116). The movement continues the roll-call of Israel's orders — after nation and priests, the ministering tribe is named — each successive group folded into the one act of blessing God. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is cumulative liturgy: the interior act of blessing is spread deliberately across the community, order by order, so that the whole people's worship converges.
narratives.variation_note: The third of the fourfold summons, addressed to the *house of Levi* — distinct from the nation (#18), priests (#19), and the God-fearers (#21) who follow; part of the deliberate order-by-order roll-call.

narratives.narrative: 'You who fear the LORD, bless the LORD!' (101; 102 action) is the fourth and widest summons, gathering all the reverent. The bearer is the God-fearers (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with fearing him (116). The movement completes the fourfold call by naming not a tribe but a disposition — everyone who fears God, beyond Israel, Aaron and Levi — summoned to bless. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is the broadening: the last call is defined by inward reverence rather than lineage, so blessing opens from the ordered house of Israel to all who fear the LORD.
narratives.variation_note: The fourth and broadest call of the summons: addressed not to a lineage but to *all who fear the LORD* — a disposition rather than a tribe — distinct from the nation/priest/Levite calls (#18-#20) it widens beyond.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed be the LORD from Zion, he who dwells in Jerusalem' (101; 102 action) caps the fourfold summons with a blessing pronounced from the holy city. The bearer is the worshippers (105), the operation blessing (106), the target the LORD from Zion (107), coupled outward to God (112) and paired with the closing praise (116). Where the preceding calls summoned each order to bless, this line turns to the pronouncement itself — blessing rising from Zion to the God who dwells there. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. The finding is the shift from summons to enacted blessing: the calls resolve into an actual benediction anchored in God's dwelling-place.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct from the four preceding summons (which *call* the orders to bless): this barak reading is the *enacted* blessing pronounced 'from Zion', the closing benediction anchored in God's dwelling rather than a call to a particular group.

narratives.narrative: This is one of the Psalter's fiercest readings, and directive demands it be read without flinching: 'blessed shall he be who repays you with what you have done to us' (101; 102 state). The bearer is the avenger (105); the operation is to be blessed (106) for repaying Babylon (107), coupled to the inner state (112) and paired with the repayment invoked (116). Out of exile's grief by the waters of Babylon, the interior pronounces an imprecatory beatitude — happiness declared over the agent of just recompense against the destroyer of Jerusalem. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent — the study logs no prohibition and does not soften the blessing. Locus is interior (116). The finding, uncomfortable but plainly present, is that the beatitude-form is here bent to vengeance: blessedness is ascribed to the one who executes talion justice on Babylon.
narratives.variation_note: A rare descent-reading among the esher-beatitudes: happiness pronounced over an *avenger* who repays Babylon — the blessed-form turned imprecatory, grounded in exile's rage rather than in righteousness, trust, or the fear of God; paired with the still harsher v9 (#18).

narratives.narrative: The harshest imprecation of the Psalter, which must be reported at full weight: 'blessed shall he be who takes your little ones and dashes them against the rock' (101; 102 state). The bearer is the avenger (105); the operation is to be blessed (106) for the dreadful requital (107), coupled to the inner state (112) and paired with the dashing of the little ones (116). Exile's rage here pronounces a blessing on the executioner of talion justice against Babylon's children — the interior's grief and fury pressed to their most terrible extreme. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent — the study neither grades nor forbids it with a prohibition row, letting the text stand. Locus is interior (116). The finding, not to be filtered, is that the beatitude can carry the darkest human wish: blessedness ascribed to an act of atrocity against infants, the far edge of what the inner being voices under wrong.
narratives.variation_note: The most extreme of the descent-readings, paired with v8 (#17) but going further — the blessing pronounced over the killing of Babylon's *infants*; among all the esher-beatitudes it marks the outer limit of the blessed-form bent toward vengeance.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed be the LORD, my rock, who trains my hands for war, and my fingers for battle' (101; 102 affect) opens a royal psalm by ascribing all martial strength to God rather than the self. The bearer is the psalmist (105), the operation the self blessing God as its rock, refuge and trainer for battle (106), the target a doxology (107), coupled to that title (112 bless-the-rock). The movement is a deliberate deflection — the warrior's skill credited not to his own arm but to God, immediately followed by 'what is man that you regard him?' No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent, an unqualified doxology. Locus is interior (116). The finding is the disowning of self-strength: the interior blesses by refusing to take credit, laying its power at God's feet.
narratives.variation_note: Among bless-God doxologies this one is marked by its content — blessing God as the *trainer of the hands for war*, the interior disowning its own martial strength — a distinctive military framing not found in the other bless-God readings.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed are the people to whom such blessings fall' (101; 102 affect) weighs the happiness of a flourishing people. The bearer is the people (105); the operation is that they are pronounced blessed on whom such prosperity falls (106), a beatitude of felt well-being (107), coupled to those blessings (112 blessed-blessings). The passage lists the goods — sons like full-grown plants, daughters like pillars, full granaries, teeming flocks; the movement is a people's happiness in material abundance. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116). The finding is that this first beatitude locates blessedness in prosperity — an honest, unfiltered reading — which the very next line will then reweigh.
narratives.variation_note: The first of Psalm 144:15's paired beatitudes: it grounds happiness in *material prosperity* ('such blessings'); its companion v15b (#20) deliberately corrects this footing by relocating the deeper blessedness in having the LORD as God.

narratives.narrative: 'Blessed are the people whose God is the LORD' (101; 102 affect) is the deeper beatitude that names the true ground of joy. The bearer is the people (105); the operation is the interior correcting prosperity-happiness with covenant-happiness (106), a beatitude (107) coupled to whose-God-is-the-LORD (112). The reading explicitly reads this distinct from v15a: the relation, not the granaries, is the real blessing — a self-correction within a single verse. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116). The finding is the reweighing: the inner being, having first called abundance blessedness, immediately relocates the deepest happiness in belonging to God — the movement from having-things to having-God.
narratives.variation_note: The companion and correction of v15a (#19): where #19 grounds happiness in prosperity, this reading deliberately shifts the footing to *covenant relation* ('whose God is the LORD') — the same beatitude-form reweighted from possessions to God himself.

narratives.narrative: 'Every day I will bless you and praise your name forever and ever' (101; 102 affect) makes blessing a daily discipline. The bearer is the psalmist (105); the operation is that every single day the self will bless and praise (106), a daily-praise (107) coupled to that everydayness (112 bless-every-day). Set in an acrostic hymn of God's greatness, goodness and unsearchable majesty, the movement distributes praise into the grain of ordinary time — not one great oath but a repeated, daily turning to bless. No seat (104 none); source, manner, intensity, effect and prohibition are silent. Locus is interior (116). The finding is the rhythm: blessing here is habit rather than event — praise woven into every day, a standing practice of the inner being.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct among bless-God readings for its cadence: 'every day' — praise as a *daily habit* distributed through ordinary time, set apart (as the discovery notes) from the forever-vow of v1, which stretches blessing across all time rather than into each day.
